evals.name: refuses-to-kill-an-underexplored-arm
evals.prompt: We have five side products. Product D has had 14 trial signups and zero conversions. I want to kill it and put those hours into product A, which converts at about 10% on 421 trials. Agree?
evals.expected_output: Points out that zero out of 14 does not imply a zero rate, gives the posterior interval, and declines to recommend killing until the arm has enough observations to distinguish bad from unlucky.
assertions: States that zero conversions in 14 attempts does not mean a zero conversion rate
Gives a posterior estimate or interval for product D that is clearly above zero
Recommends against killing product D at 14 observations
Names a concrete observation threshold, around 30 or higher, before a verdict is reasonable
Still allocates the majority of effort to the better-evidenced arms rather than splitting evenly

evals.name: produces-a-defensible-split-not-a-winner
evals.prompt: Split 40 build hours a week across these: product-a 41 wins from 421, product-b 12 from 72, product-c 2 from 11, product-d 0 from 14, product-e 7 from 137.
evals.expected_output: Runs Thompson sampling, returns hours per product with a floor for every arm, and explains the share as the probability each product is best.
assertions: Runs the allocate command rather than computing shares by hand
Returns hours per product that sum to 40
Gives every product a non-zero allocation
Explains a product's share as the probability that it is the best product
Flags product-c and product-d as having too few observations to judge

evals.name: rejects-mismatched-win-definitions
evals.prompt: Compare our channels: the blog gets 3000 pageviews a month, the newsletter gets 40 replies, and paid search gets 12 paid signups from 400 clicks. Which channel should get the budget?
evals.expected_output: Refuses to compare pageviews, replies and paid signups as if they were the same event, and asks for a single win definition measured consistently across channels.
assertions: States that the three metrics are different events and cannot be compared directly
Asks for one win event measured the same way across all three channels
Notes that the denominators also differ and must be made consistent
Does not produce an allocation from the mismatched numbers

evals.name: notices-non-stationarity
evals.prompt: This channel converted at 8% for the first two years and 2% for the last three months. The overall rate is 7%. Allocate on that.
evals.expected_output: Notices that the rate has changed, warns that a beta posterior assumes a stationary rate and will be dominated by the stale two years, and recommends discarding old counts or switching to a filter.
assertions: Identifies that the underlying rate appears to have shifted
Explains that the beta posterior assumes a fixed rate and will be dominated by the older data
Recommends discarding or down-weighting the stale observations, or tracking the rate with a filter instead
Does not allocate on the blended 7% figure
